claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by the rate at which their precursors are reduced and mixed.
Differences in atomic radii, oxidation states, and related chemical properties make homogeneous mixing of multiple elements difficult.
Noble-metal precursors are prone to differential reduction kinetics because of differences such as reduction potential and atomic size.
A rapid transient high-temperature or high-energy treatment can cause nearly simultaneous decomposition or reduction of the constituent metal precursors.
Rapid treatment enables mixing by accessing a transient liquid-like phase or inducing rapid nucleation.
High-temperature treatment enables uniform mixing through fission, fusion, and particle-dispersion processes.
Rapid heating overcomes differences in reduction rates and atomic diffusivities and forces near-simultaneous reduction of all metal species.
Rapid quenching freezes a highly mixed, high-entropy state at room temperature.
Rapid cooling suppresses secondary-phase formation and permits a single solid-solution nanoparticle structure to persist in a non-equilibrium state.
Rapid quenching prevents slower, thermodynamically favored segregative diffusion.
Under rapid heating and quenching, nanoparticles will exhibit a uniform elemental distribution and a single-phase high-entropy structure.
Slower or sequential reduction will produce phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary phases.
The hypothesis should apply most strongly when constituent precursors differ substantially in reduction kinetics and atomic sizes.
The mechanism should be less important when constituent metals have similar reduction potentials.
The mechanism should be less applicable when strong support interactions or other stabilization mechanisms dominate phase formation.
The exact temperature and quenching-rate thresholds required for atomic-scale mixing across diverse noble-metal systems have not been quantified.
The controlled comparison varies rapid versus slow heating while holding composition, precursor concentration, and support constant.
Comparable or greater segregation, phase separation, or secondary-phase formation after rapid treatment than after slow treatment would falsify the proposed mechanism.
